author: Asterius of Amasea
addressee: a congregation gathered for the feast of the martyr Phocas
occasion: A festal homily delivered at a shrine of the martyr Phocas, celebrating his witness and encouraging devotion to him.
argument: Asterius opens by saying that all martyrs are holy, but they do not all receive equal glory or equal honors; the first and second place distinction applies even among saints, because the judge's assessment is exact and unswerving, apportioning rewards according to each one's contest. He then presents Phocas as a martyr of surpassing fame, known everywhere like the sun's ray. The homily recounts how Phocas, a gardener near Sinope, practiced hospitality, and how soldiers sent to arrest him lodged with him without recognizing him or being recognized; when they revealed their mission, Phocas prepared his own tomb and then identified himself to them. After his beheading, his shrine became a source of relief, healing, and food for the poor, and his relics were honored in many places, including the imperial city and Rome. The homily closes by describing sailors' custom of setting aside a share for Phocas, the veneration of barbarian peoples, and a barbarian king's dedication of his crown and breastplate, before ending with praise to God.

outline.move: Asterius introduces the feast at the shrine of Phocas, where he is physically present; he mentions that being at the place fills him with memory of all the stories told about Phocas, argues that martyrs receive unequal honors according to their contests, presents Phocas as a martyr of surpassing fame, and begins the story of his life as a hospitable gardener near Sinope and the arrival of soldiers seeking him.

The soldiers lodge with Phocas without recognizing him, and after being moved by his hospitality they first make him swear to tell no one, then reveal their secret mission; Phocas promises to find the man they seek, prepares his own tomb, and the next day reveals that he himself is Phocas.

The soldiers are stunned, but Phocas urges them to carry out their orders; he is beheaded, and Asterius praises his shrine as a source of relief and food for the poor, and describes the spread of his relics and his honor in the imperial city and Rome.

Asterius describes the sailors' custom of reserving a daily share for Phocas and giving the money to the poor, the veneration of Phocas by emperors and barbarian peoples, a barbarian king's dedication of his crown and breastplate, and closes with doxology.

scripture: The author cites the Psalms according to the Septuagint numbering and alludes to biblical narratives without formal citation formulas. Modern citations should use standard English Bible book names and, for Psalms, the Hebrew numbering with a note where the Septuagint numbering differs.
uncertain: The precise date of the homily is not stated in the text.
The exact location of the shrine where the homily was delivered is not named in the text.
The identity of the barbarian king who dedicated the crown and breastplate is not given.
Whether the 'imperial city' refers to Constantinople or Rome is not explicitly stated in the text.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Asterius introduces the feast at the shrine of Phocas, where he is physically present
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: εὐθὺς γὰρ ἐν τῷ τιμίῳ τούτου σήκῳ γενόμενος καὶ τῇ ἱερᾷ θήκῃ τοῦ σώματος προσψαύων ἐκ τοῦ τόπου πληροῦμαι τῆς μνήμης
_unresolved_facts.fix: Asterius mentions being at the shrine (σῆκος) and touching the sacred coffin, but does not explicitly state this is where he delivers the homily; the location of delivery is not named

_unresolved_facts.claim: the first and second place distinction applies even among saints
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἀλλὰ τὸ πρῶτον καὶ δεύτερον οὐδὲ ὁ τῶν ἁγίων ἐκφεύγει κατάλογος
_unresolved_facts.fix: the first and second place distinction does not escape even the catalogue of saints

_unresolved_facts.claim: they first make him swear to tell no one
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: μηδενί τε τὸ λεχθησόμενον ἐξειπεῖν παραγγείλαντες
_unresolved_facts.fix: they instruct him to tell no one (they make him promise secrecy, not swear an oath)

_unresolved_facts.claim: Phocas promises to find the man they seek
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Κἀγώ, φησίν, ὑμῖν εἰς τὸ προκείμενον συνεφάψομαι. Γινώσκω γὰρ τὸν ἄνδρα καὶ ῥᾳδίως ἀναζητήσας εὑρήσω
_unresolved_facts.fix: Phocas says he will 'join in helping' (συνεφάψομαι) with their task and will search for and find the man

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἐπλήγησαν τὰς ψυχὰς οἱ ἄνθρωποι καὶ πρὸς τὴν ἀκοὴν ἀπεπάγησαν
_unresolved_facts.fix: the men were struck in their souls and frozen at the hearing

_unresolved_facts.claim: Joseph... who sold grain for silver in Egypt while alive
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἐκεῖνος μὲν γὰρ ἀργυρίου τὸν σῖτον διήμειβεν, οὗτος δὲ προῖκα τοῖς δεομένοις χαρίζεται
_unresolved_facts.fix: Joseph who exchanged grain for silver in Egypt previously (τὸ πρότερον), not 'while alive'

_unresolved_facts.claim: introduced by εἰπόντων and ἐκ περιχαρείας (with joy/exultation)
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Τῶν δὲ εἰπόντων ἐκ περιχαρείας· Καὶ ποῦ ὁ ἀνήρ;
_unresolved_facts.fix: introduced by εἰπόντων with ἐκ περιχαρείας indicating the manner of speaking (with great joy), not the speaker identification

_unresolved_facts.claim: the western ocean: the Atlantic Ocean
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὅσοι τὸν ὠκεανὸν πλέουσι τὸν ἑσπέριον

_unresolved_facts.claim: the Maeotic lake: the Sea of Azov
_unresolved_facts.fix: the Maeotic lake (modern identification as Sea of Azov is reasonable but not explicit in text)

_unresolved_facts.claim: the river Tanais: the Don River
_unresolved_facts.fix: the river Tanais (modern identification as Don River is reasonable but not explicit in text)

_unresolved_facts.claim: the river Phasis: the Phasis River

_unresolved_facts.claim: Whether the 'imperial city' refers to Constantinople or Rome is not explicitly stated in the text
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Οὕτω γοῦν καὶ κατὰ τὴν βασιλεύουσαν πόλιν, τὴν κορυφὴν Ἰταλίας καὶ βασιλίδα τοῦ κόσμου
_unresolved_facts.fix: The 'imperial city' is explicitly identified as 'the peak of Italy and queen of the world' — this is Rome, not ambiguous
